lead: Class C conducts for less than half a cycle, and class D conducts either fully on or fully off. Both keep the transistor out of the region where it carries high current and high voltage at the same time, so efficiency rises. Class C uses a tuned LC tank to rebuild the sine wave and drives radio transmitters. Class D switches at a high frequency, carries the signal as pulse width, and filters the result; it drives audio amplifiers, phone speakers and motor drives.
prereq: You need: the push-pull idea of two devices driving one load (Chapter 3.6), the conduction-angle and efficiency comparison of classes A, B and C (Chapter 3.5), and the diode and switch basics from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Class C: less than half a cycle, and a tuned load

blocks.text: A class C stage is biased far below cut-off. In an npn transistor the base is held below the emitter, so the device stays off until the input peak swings it on. Current then flows in a short pulse once per cycle, for less than half the input cycle. The conduction angle is the part of the 360° input cycle during which the device conducts. For class C it is less than 180°, and RF designs commonly use 90° to 150°.

Efficiency rises because a transistor dissipates power only when voltage across it and current through it are both present. In class C the device carries zero current for most of the cycle, so the average dissipation is small. Practical class C stages reach 60 % to 80 %. For comparison, a class B stage peaks near 78.5 % at full drive and a class A stage peaks at about 25 % with a resistive load (up to 50 % with a transformer-coupled load).

The transistor current is a narrow pulse train, not a sine. The load is a parallel LC tank resonant at the carrier frequency f₀. The tank has high impedance at f₀ and low impedance elsewhere, so the voltage across it is almost a pure sine at f₀. The tank does the wave shaping; the transistor only supplies pulses of energy.

blocks.where: f₀ is the resonant frequency in hertz, L is the tank inductance in henries, C is the tank capacitance in farads. At f₀ the tank impedance is maximum and the output is a sine.

blocks.text: Class C works only over a narrow band around f₀. The transistor current is a narrow pulse train rich in harmonics, and only the f₀ component appears as a large sine at the tank; the harmonics are mostly suppressed. Any signal whose energy moves outside that narrow band appears as severe distortion. FM and CW transmitters keep a constant envelope and a fixed carrier, so class C is often their final stage. Audio cannot use it: speech and music spread over 20 Hz to 20 kHz and change amplitude constantly, so a tank tuned to one frequency would distort them.

sections.h3: Class D: switch, do not amplify

blocks.text: In class D the transistor never sits between on and off. It is either fully on, with the voltage across it near zero and current set by the load, or fully off, with current zero and full voltage across it. Instantaneous dissipation p = v × i is small in both states, so almost no heat is made and almost all the DC input reaches the load.

The signal is carried as pulse width modulation (PWM). A comparator compares the audio input with a triangle carrier at the switching frequency, usually a few hundred kilohertz. A large audio sample gives a wide pulse, a small sample a narrow pulse, so the duty cycle D follows the audio.

blocks.where: v_avg is the average of the switched waveform over one switching period in volts, D is the duty cycle (0 to 1, no unit), V_DD is the supply voltage in volts. The LC filter produces this average at the load.

blocks.text: The PWM drives two MOSFETs in a half-bridge, one pulling the output to V_DD and the other to ground — the push-pull action of Chapter 3.6. Both must never conduct together, so a small dead time separates them. The square wave then enters an LC low-pass filter whose cut-off lies between the audio band (20 kHz) and the switching frequency. The filter averages the pulses, the carrier is removed, and only audio reaches the speaker.

Ideal efficiency is 100 %, because ideal switches dissipate nothing. Real losses are switching loss during each transition, conduction loss in the on-resistance R_ds(on), gate-drive power, inductor resistance and the dead time. Practical class D amplifiers reach 85 % to 95 %, against 50 % to 70 % for a class AB amplifier of the same output power.

blocks.text: Two more switching classes exist. Class E shapes the voltage across the switch with a resonant load so that it falls to zero before the device turns on, called zero-voltage switching. Class F tunes the harmonics of its output network to build a flatter voltage waveform. Both are RF techniques; the names are enough here.

items: Battery life: a 90 % efficient amplifier turns one-tenth of the DC power into heat, so a phone speaker plays longer and stays cool.
Motor drives: the same comparator and bridge form an inverter, and the PWM averages into a sine current in the motor winding.
Bandwidth: the LC low-pass passes the whole audio band, while a class C tank passes only a narrow slice around f₀.

figure.caption: The audio input and the triangle carrier meet in the comparator, whose pulse-width output drives the MOSFET pair; the LC filter removes the carrier so that only audio reaches the speaker.

spec.aria: Class D: an audio signal and a triangle carrier drive a comparator, whose PWM output switches MOSFETs; the LC filter removes the carrier and leaves the audio at the load.

examples.question: A class D audio amplifier delivers 20 W of audio to a load. Its switching MOSFETs dissipate 1 W and its LC filter dissipates 0.5 W. Find the total loss, the DC input power and the conversion efficiency.
steps: Losses add up: P_loss = P_MOS + P_filter = 1 W + 0.5 W = 1.5 W.
Energy conservation: P_DC = P_load + P_loss = 20 W + 1.5 W = 21.5 W.
Check: 1.5 W lost is 6.98 % of the input, a realistic class D figure and far better than the 50 % to 70 % of class AB.
examples.answer: The loss is 1.5 W, the DC input power is 21.5 W, and the conversion efficiency is 93.0 %.
examples.check:
P_load = 20.0
P_mos = 1.0
P_filter = 0.5
P_loss = P_mos + P_filter
P_dc = P_load + P_loss
eta = P_load / P_dc * 100
print(P_loss)
print(P_dc)
print(round(eta, 1))

traps: Quoting class D as 100 % efficient. That is the ideal-switch figure; switching, conduction, gate-drive and filter losses bring real circuits to 85 % to 95 %.
Swapping the two load networks. A class C tank is resonant at the carrier and rebuilds the sine; a class D LC section is a low-pass filter that removes the carrier and passes the audio.
Forgetting that P_DC = P_load + P_loss. Putting P_DC = P_load gives 100 %, and inverting the ratio (P_DC / P_load) gives a number above 1.
Claiming class C suits audio because its efficiency is high. Its output is a pulse train restored by a narrowband tank, so amplitude and frequency changes are destroyed.

quiz.q: Define conduction angle and state its range for class C.
quiz.a: The portion of the 360° input cycle during which the device carries current. For class C it is less than 180°, commonly 90° to 150° in RF work.

quiz.q: Why does a class C stage need a tuned LC load, and what exactly does that load do?
quiz.a: The transistor current is a narrow pulse train containing f₀ and many harmonics. The parallel tank has high impedance at f₀ and low impedance elsewhere, so harmonic currents produce almost no voltage while the f₀ component produces the full sine.

quiz.q: Why is the dissipation of a class D stage small in both switch states?
quiz.a: Dissipation is p = v × i. On state: voltage near zero. Off state: current zero. The device never sits in the high-voltage, high-current region that a class A or AB transistor passes through.

quiz.q: A class D amplifier delivers 50 W. The MOSFETs lose 2 W and the filter loses 1 W. Find the efficiency.
A class D half-bridge runs from V_DD = 24 V with duty cycle D = 0.4 at one instant. Find the average voltage at the filter input.
quiz.a: v_avg = D × V_DD = 0.4 × 24 V = 9.6 V. The LC filter delivers this average to the load at that instant.

quiz.q: Explain why class C is unsuitable for an audio power amplifier even though its efficiency is high.
quiz.a: Conduction is under half a cycle, so the output is a pulse train whose shape depends on the tank, and the tank restores a sine only near f₀. Audio spans 20 Hz to 20 kHz with continuously changing amplitude, so most components fall outside the tank band and appear as severe distortion.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gallium nitride (GaN) MOSFETs switch faster with less charge, pushing switching frequencies into the megahertz range and shrinking the filter. Self-oscillating and sigma-delta class D designs correct distortion with feedback instead of trimming components. In electric vehicles the same bridge-plus-PWM idea becomes a three-phase motor inverter, where efficiency buys range.
